title: Morphological and palaeoecological aspects of fossil insects unveiled by UV-A light
author: Boderau, Jouault, et al.

steps.title: Gather equipment and safety gear
steps.instruction: Collect a compact portable UV‑A lamp (emits at 370 nm, measured λmax = 371 nm), an adapted band‑pass filter for the LED flashlight, UV‑protective safety glasses, a camera (e.g., Nikon Z7 II) mounted on a statif rail or a stereomicroscope (e.g., Nikon SMZ25), macro lenses equipped with UV filters, a computer with photo‑editing software, an Avantes AVASpec 2048SL spectrophotometer, and a MEB FEG TESCAN CLARA scanning electron microscope capable of dual‑EDS in variable‑pressure mode.

steps.title: Prepare dark imaging station and camera
steps.instruction: Place the setup in a completely dark room (e.g., a basement). Wear the UV‑protective glasses. Mount the camera on the chosen support, attach the macro lens with its UV filter, and increase the ISO setting to a high value to maximise photon capture. Ensure the camera is connected to the photo‑editing software for later processing.

steps.title: Illuminate specimen with UV‑A and acquire fluorescence images
steps.instruction: Turn on the commercial LED flashlight equipped with the band‑pass filter; verify its emission peak (vendor‑stated 365 nm, measured 371 nm). Position the lamp so that the fossil is uniformly illuminated with 371 nm UV‑A light. Capture photographs of the specimen, adjusting exposure as needed while keeping the camera settings constant.

steps.title: Record fluorescence emission spectra
steps.instruction: Using the Avantes AVASpec 2048SL spectrophotometer, place the fiber probe on at least two points: one on the fossil material and one on the surrounding sedimentary matrix. Acquire emission spectra under the 371 nm excitation and save the raw data for each point.

steps.title: Perform elemental analysis by EDS
steps.instruction: Load the same specimen into the MEB FEG TESCAN CLARA SEM. Set the instrument to dual‑EDS mode and enable variable‑pressure mode to allow imaging of non‑conductive, non‑metallised samples. Acquire secondary‑electron (SE) and back‑scattered electron (BSE) images, then collect EDS spectra at the identical points used for fluorescence measurements to obtain elemental maps of the fossil and matrix.

steps.title: Process spectral data
steps.instruction: Normalize each fluorescence spectrum, calculate the differential spectrum between fossil and matrix, and convert the normalized spectra to CIE 1931 colour coordinates. Record the resulting coordinates: fossil (x = 0.310483694, y = 0.370985016) and matrix (x = 0.294099197, y = 0.352832879).

steps.title: Optional comparative imaging under alternative light sources
steps.instruction: Photograph the same specimen under three illumination conditions: (i) normal white light, (ii) UV‑A light at 371 nm, and (iii) violet light at 395 nm using the Nikon Z7 II attached to the Nikon SMZ25 stereomicroscope. Keep camera settings identical across the three sessions to allow direct contrast comparison.

description: Equipment and setup for simple UV-light observation of insect fossils. The equipment needed for examining fossil insects under UV light is simple: at least a compact, affordable, portable lamp emitting UV-A light at 370 nm; a pair of UV-light protective safety glasses; a photographic setup combining either a camera mounted on a statif rail or a stereomicroscope, macro lenses equipped with UV filters; a software for photo editing (Fig. 1).Fig. 1Setup designed for UV-light photography of insect fossils for (A) a stereomicroscope and (B) a statif rail.Fig. 1 Maximum wavelength of the UV-A light source. In this study, a commercial LED flashlight, equipped with an adapted band pass filter, was used as the UV-A light source. A maximum wavelength (λmax) of 365 nm was indicated by the vendor. However, upon measuring its emission spectrum with a calibrated Avantes AVASpec 2048SL spectrophotometer, it was necessary to correct the value of λmax to 371 nm (Figure S-1, suppl. inf.). This corrected maximum wavelength falls within the UV-A range of the electromagnetic spectrum, and significantly differs from the other light sources typically utilized in other invertebrate palaeontological studies. In contrast, those studies commonly employ lasers with maximum wavelengths in the visible blue range [6,13]. Natural fluorescence. The methodology is based on the concept of natural fluorescence, often referred to as “autofluorescence” or “epifluorescence” in the context of microscopic techniques. This optical intrinsic property is inherent to various natural materials such as minerals or organic and inorganic bio-matter [15]. Fluorescence, the most common type of photo-luminescence, is defined as the spontaneous light emission upon photo-excitation. When a fossil is illuminated with light of a specific wavelength, it emits light of a different wavelength, which possesses less energy than the initial excitation wavelength.
